Origination and outreach, for M&A desks

Nothing slips. Nothing walks out the door.

Boutique M&A desks run origination on three spreadsheets and an inbox. Upstream is those three sheets joined up: the master list, the follow-up clock and the contact history, held by the firm instead of by whoever still works here.

Four ways a mandate quietly costs you money.

None of these are hypothetical. They are the failures the desk this was built for hit often enough to go and build something.

  • Two analysts email the same CFO.

    One sheet per mandate and no way to check across them. The firm finds out from the target, which is the expensive way to find out.

    How the check works→

  • The follow-up date passes on a Tuesday.

    Nobody had the schedule open. By the time someone does, the thread is three weeks cold and reopening it costs a favour.

    The follow-up clock→

  • Every mandate rebuilds the same knowledge.

    Somebody here has worked this buyer before and knows how they responded. That sits in an inbox, or in their head, and neither is searchable.

    What the second mandate knows→

  • An analyst leaves on Friday.

    Their relationships, their context and half the reason a buyer took the last call walk out with them. The firm paid for all of it.

    Where the relationships live→

    The second mandate should know what the first one learned.

    One sheet per mandate means the firm forgets everything the moment a deal closes. Upstream keeps the record at the firm, so it compounds instead.

    1. The firm is the unit, not the mandate

      Every company, contact and touch belongs to the firm first and the mandate second. That one decision in the data model is what makes the rest of this possible.

      Step 1 of 3

    2. A name already in play gets flagged

      Before anyone sends, Upstream checks the name against every other live mandate, near-matches included, and shows what happened the last time the firm approached them.

      Step 2 of 3

    3. The second mandate starts ahead of the first

      A buyer you approached in March opens in September with their history attached: who reached them, what they said, and whether they were worth the call.

      Step 3 of 3

    Two people have to say yes, and they want opposite things.

    The analyst is judged on speed. The partner is judged on nothing going wrong. The same record has to satisfy both or the rollout stalls in week three.

    The daily userAnalyst / Associate

    Faster than the spreadsheet, or it does not get used.

    This one is not sentimental. If it costs an analyst more keystrokes than the sheet did, the sheet wins and the rollout is over.

    • One queue, worst first, no filtering required
    • Log a touch, draft a mail or push a date from the row
    • Several people on one mandate without a merge conflict
    • The fields your template already has, in the order you had them
    The economic buyerPartner / Managing Director

    Nothing slipping, and nothing embarrassing.

    The partner is not going to open this daily. They need it to answer the two questions they currently answer by walking over and asking.

    • Every live mandate's health, without requesting a status update
    • Duplicate outreach stopped before it reaches the market
    • Contacted through to interested, as one funnel per mandate
    • The firm keeps the relationships when the analyst does not

    Narrow on purpose.

    Upstream does the upstream stage of a mandate and stops. That is a decision, not a gap, and it is the reason the thing is fast enough that an analyst will actually use it on a Tuesday.

    What it does
    • Origination and outreach for a live mandate
    • Three spreadsheets, joined into one firm-wide record
    • A follow-up cadence that computes itself
    • Contact memory that outlives the mandate and the analyst

    Four lines. That is the whole surface, which is why an analyst can learn it between two calls instead of between two quarters.

    What it does not

    • Mass email and automated sending

      Not planned. Sending is one at a time, on purpose

    • Valuation models, teasers, NDA generation

      Not planned

    • NDA tracking, bid management, diligence

      Midstream. After the desk is running on this

    • Competing with enterprise deal platforms

      Not the wedge. See below

    Where that puts it

    • Enterprise deal platforms

      Configurable relationship and deal management, built for large PE and IB.

      Six figures a year and a quarter to roll out. Priced and paced for a firm ten times your size.

    • Sourcing databases

      Company search, firmographics and signals. Genuinely good at finding names.

      They hand you a list. They do not run the outreach or remember what came of it.

    • Upstream

      The outreach workflow itself, built from the sheets a boutique desk already runs.

      Narrow on purpose. It does the one job that costs you deals when it goes wrong.

    Days to live, not a quarter.

    Enterprise deal platforms quote implementation in months because they have to be configured into a shape your firm recognises. This already is that shape.

    1. 01
      Week one

      We move the sheets, not you

      Onboarding is the migration. Your columns get mapped, the duplicates already sitting in the files get shown to you, and one live mandate goes in first so you can hold it against the spreadsheet it came from.

    2. 02
      The same week

      One mandate runs on it

      Not the whole book. One mandate, in parallel with the sheet, until the analyst on it stops opening the sheet. That usually takes a few days and it is the only adoption test that means anything.

    3. 03
      The mandate after

      The closed ones start paying

      Load the mandates you have already closed. That is where the contact intelligence is, and it is what makes the cross-mandate check useful immediately rather than a year from now.

    Who you are talking to is the whole secret.

    A live buyer list is the most commercially sensitive thing a desk holds. It was locked down at the data model, not bolted on before a security review.

    • httpOnly, Secure cookies. No token is ever readable from the browser
    • Refresh tokens rotate, and revoke server-side. Log out everywhere at once
    • Firm-scoped at the query, so an analyst cannot address a mandate they are not on
    • Nothing is deleted. Records are archived, which is also why history survives
    • Password hashes never leave the server

    One clock, wherever the counterparty sits.

    Buyers are rarely in the same timezone as the desk chasing them. Due-dates resolve on one shared clock, so “overdue” means the same thing to the analyst in Mumbai and the partner reading the queue from London.

    Illustrative. The hub is wherever your desk is

    Everything teams ask before moving off spreadsheets.

    Still curious? Book a demo

    • Because the spreadsheets work right up until they don't: a file gets overwritten, a mandate closes and its sheet is archived somewhere, an analyst leaves. Upstream is those exact sheets with the fragility removed. The fields, the buckets and the cadence are the ones you already use.

    • Days, not a quarter, because there is nothing to configure into a shape you recognise. It already is that shape. The week-one sequence is on this page above.

    • Bring them. Closed mandates are where most of the contact intelligence is, and loading them is what makes the cross-mandate layer useful on day one rather than in a year.

    • It sends from your mailbox, one message at a time, when you press send. There is no relay, no shared sending domain and no bulk send. Your deliverability stays yours, and a target never receives something that reads like a campaign.

    • No. Scoping happens at the query, not by hiding buttons. Partners see the whole book plus analytics and escalation.

    • Upstream covers origination and outreach deliberately, and stops there. Midstream execution is the next stage, not a checkbox we have quietly shipped. If you need bid management today, we are the wrong tool today.

    • You do, and yes. Export is not a retention lever. Records are archived rather than deleted, so the export includes the full history rather than the current state of a row.

    • Auth uses httpOnly, Secure cookies, so no token is ever readable from the browser. Refresh tokens rotate and can be revoked server-side. We do not claim certifications we have not been through.

    Bring one mandate. Keep the spreadsheet open.

    We will migrate one live mandate and run it beside the sheet it came from. If the analyst on it still opens the sheet after a week, we have not earned the rest.
